posts.hook: A free guide: Protein, decoded
Where does your fibre come from?
posts.li:
We've just published a free 34-page guide for anyone who explains food to other people: Protein, decoded.

It started with a question we hear every week from learners and their clients: how much protein do I need, and where does it come from on an Indian plate?

Every number in it comes from Indian government sources: ICMR-NIN's Nutrient Requirements (2020), the Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024), the Indian Food Composition Tables and FSSAI's labelling rules. There are no brand tie-ins and no supplement advice.

It includes a 60-second self-check, an Indian food table, eight easy wins and a weekly tracker.

posts.hook: What 500 g of vegetables and fruit looks like
posts.li:
400 g of vegetables and 100 g of fruit a day. That's the reference ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) use for a 2,000 kcal day, with vegetables, greens and fruit making up about half the plate.

In counselling, the number lands better when people can see it. Two katoris of sabzi, a bowl of salad, a plate of greens and one fruit gets most people there.

The other half of the plate is where protein comes in, and that's what our free guide covers.

posts.li:
Dhanteras is a day for investing in what lasts.

ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) estimate that 56.4% of the total disease burden in India is due to unhealthy diets. The same report says healthy diets and physical activity can prevent up to 80% of type 2 diabetes.

That's why we think nutrition literacy is worth investing in, for professionals and for families. Our free guide is a practical place to start.

posts.hook: Four colours for this week's shopping list
Happy Diwali from all of us at NNWA
posts.ig:
Happy Diwali from all of us at NNWA.

Tonight, kitchens across India will be full: the kaju katli someone's mother still makes by hand, the chakli that never lasts till morning, the plate kept aside for the neighbours.

Enjoy all of it. If you're frying at home, one tip from ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024): filter the oil once you've finished frying, use it for curries over the next day or two, and don't fry with it again.

May your home be bright and your table be shared.

Happy Diwali from everyone at NNWA (Nutrition & Wellness Academy).

posts.hook: Learn it. Apply it.
posts.ig:
Learn it. Apply it.

Festive season is when everyone has nutrition advice: what to skip, what to 'detox' with, what someone's cousin swears by. Knowing what the evidence actually says, and how to explain it to someone you care about, is a skill.

NNWA (Nutrition & Wellness Academy) teaches it 100% online, from a short introduction to full certifications and diplomas, with every lesson grounded in Indian guidelines.
posts.li:
After a week of festive tables, the questions start: what should I cut, should I detox, is this supplement worth it?

Answering those well takes more than a list of rules. It takes knowing the evidence, and the Indian guidelines behind it, well enough to explain it simply.

That's what NNWA (Nutrition & Wellness Academy) teaches, 100% online, from short courses to full certifications and diplomas.

posts.hook: This Bhai Dooj, gift a habit
posts.ig:
This Bhai Dooj, gift a habit.

The tilak, the sweets, the gift you've been hiding since Dhanteras. Add one more thing this year, something you can do together.

Slide 2: a walk. ICMR-NIN suggests adults get 30 to 60 minutes of moderate activity a day, at least five days a week. A brisk evening walk with your sibling counts.
Slide 3: a box of nuts and seeds alongside the mithai. The Dietary Guidelines for Indians list nuts and seeds as the swap for deep-fried snacks.
Slide 4: one home-cooked meal, with half the plate vegetables and fruit.

Habits last longer than sweets do.

posts.hook: 20 to 25 g of sugar a day
posts.li:
A useful number for the post-festival conversation: ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) advise adults to avoid added sugar or keep it to 20 to 25 g a day.

For many clients, that's a single piece of mithai plus sugar in two cups of tea. Showing them that is more useful than telling them to 'cut down'.

Our free guide uses the same approach for protein: one clear number and what it looks like on an Indian plate.

posts.hook: The kadhai of oil from Diwali: fry again or not?
posts.ig:
Is the kadhai of oil from Diwali frying still sitting on the stove?

ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) are clear on this. Heating oil again and again creates harmful compounds. Once you've fried in it, filter it, use it for curries within a day or two, and don't fry with it again.

The guidelines also suggest 25 to 30 g of cooking oil a day in total, which is about five to six teaspoons.
posts.cta_line: More practical kitchen numbers are in our free guide. Link in bio.
posts.li:
One of the most common kitchen habits in India is also one of the easiest to fix: reusing frying oil.

ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) note that repeatedly heated oil forms harmful compounds. Their household advice: filter oil after frying, use it for curries within a day or two, and don't fry with it again. They suggest 25 to 30 g of cooking oil a day in total.

It's a simple message that families can act on the same evening.

posts.hook: Children's Day: what the numbers ask of us
posts.ig:
Happy Children's Day.

Think of the youngest children in your family, the ones who refuse dal and steal the jalebi. Now look at slide 2.

According to national survey data reported in ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024), 40.6% of children aged 1 to 4 have anaemia, as do 23.5% of those aged 5 to 9 and 28.4% of those aged 10 to 19. About 1 in 10 children aged 5 to 19 already shows pre-diabetes.

What helps, per the same guidelines: varied home-cooked food, homemade semi-solid foods from six months, and at least 60 minutes of active play a day.

If you work with children or parents, our Child & Adolescent Nutrition course covers this properly.

posts.hook: World Diabetes Day: 15.6% of men, 13.5% of women
posts.ig:
World Diabetes Day.

NFHS-5 (2021) data, reported in ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024), found diabetes in 15.6% of men and 13.5% of women aged 18 to 69. In 2016 the figures were 10.5% and 9.7%.

The same guidelines say healthy diets and physical activity can prevent up to 80% of type 2 diabetes. That's why counselling and education matter so much.

If you want to help people manage diabetes day to day, NNWA's Diabetes Educator course is 100% online.

If you have diabetes, follow your doctor's advice; this post is general information.
posts.li:
World Diabetes Day. Two numbers from NFHS-5 (2021), reported in ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024): diabetes in 15.6% of men and 13.5% of women aged 18 to 69, up from 10.5% and 9.7% in 2016.

The same guidelines state that healthy diets and physical activity can prevent up to 80% of type 2 diabetes. Prevention at that scale depends on people who can explain food clearly and consistently.

NNWA's Diabetes Educator course trains exactly that, 100% online.

posts.hook: Is a nutrition course right for you? Five honest questions
posts.ig:
Thinking about studying nutrition? Answer these five questions honestly first.

1. Do you enjoy explaining things to people?
2. Are you comfortable checking a claim against a source before you share it?
3. Can you set aside a few hours a week for steady study?
4. Do you know which group you want to help: families, athletes, people with diabetes, children?
5. Are you clear that a course gives you knowledge and a certificate, and that work comes from what you do with it?

If most answers are yes, have a look at NNWA's courses. They're 100% online, and a counsellor can help you pick one.
posts.li:
Before anyone enrols with us, we'd rather they asked themselves five honest questions. Do they enjoy explaining things? Will they check a claim against its source? Can they give a few hours a week? Do they know who they want to help? And do they understand that a certificate is a start, not a guarantee of work?

We think clear expectations make better nutrition professionals. The document has all five questions.

posts.hook: The first six months: breast milk only
posts.ig:
It's National Newborn Week (15 to 21 November).

ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, with breastfeeding continuing to two years and beyond. Soon after six months, babies should start homemade semi-solid foods alongside it.

Every new mother deserves support with this, from family, from health workers and from people trained to give good advice.

NNWA's Post-Pregnancy & Lactation Nutrition course is for anyone who wants to give that support properly. 100% online.

For medical concerns about your baby, please speak to your paediatrician.
posts.li:
National Newborn Week runs from 15 to 21 November. The Dietary Guidelines for Indians (ICMR-NIN, 2024) keep the core message simple: exclusive breastfeeding for six months, homemade semi-solid foods soon after six months, and breastfeeding continued to two years and beyond.

Mothers are more likely to follow the guidance when the people around them understand it too. NNWA's Post-Pregnancy & Lactation Nutrition course is built for those people.

posts.hook: Why every number we post comes from ICMR-NIN
posts.ig:
Why does every NNWA post cite ICMR-NIN, FSSAI or the Ministry of Health?

Because nutrition advice online is full of numbers nobody can trace. We only use figures from Indian government sources, and we tell you where to find them, so you can check us.

Try it: the Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) are a free PDF on ICMR-NIN's website. Look up the 5 g salt limit yourself.

Our free guide follows the same rule, with a full source list at the back.
posts.cta_line: Get it from the link in bio.
posts.li:
A note on how we write. Every number NNWA publishes, on social media, in our free guide and in our courses, comes from an Indian government source: ICMR-NIN, ICMR, FSSAI or the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

It means saying less than we could, and leaving out claims we can't trace. We think that's what trust in health education requires.

posts.hook: International Men's Day: 1 in 4 men
posts.ig:
International Men's Day. A number worth a conversation at home.

NFHS-5 (2021), as reported in ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024), found hypertension in 24.0% of men aged 18 to 69, up from 20.2% in 2016.

Two things from the same guidelines that help: not more than 5 g of salt a day, and 30 to 60 minutes of moderate activity on at least five days a week.

If someone you love hasn't had his blood pressure checked in a while, today's a good day to suggest it.
posts.cta_line: Our free guide is in the link in bio.
posts.li:
International Men's Day. NFHS-5 (2021) data, reported in ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024), found hypertension in 24.0% of Indian men aged 18 to 69, up from 20.2% in 2016.

Most of the levers are everyday ones: salt under 5 g a day and 30 to 60 minutes of moderate activity on most days. Workplace wellness programmes can make both easier.

posts.hook: A fifth to a third of your cereals: millets
posts.ig:
How much of your roti and rice should be millets? ICMR-NIN has a number.

The Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) suggest that 20% to 30% of the cereals adults eat (by raw weight) come from millets.

In practice, that could be a bajra or jowar roti at one meal, ragi in your dosa batter, or a millet khichdi once or twice a week.

Pair millets with dal and you get a better protein mix too. That's covered in chapter 4 of our free guide.
posts.li:
A practical target from ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024): 20% to 30% of adults' cereals, by raw weight, should come from millets.

It's easier to act on than 'eat more millets'. Swapping one roti or one rice meal a day gets most households close.

posts.hook: Protein powder to build muscle? ICMR-NIN says no
posts.ig:
"Without whey you can't build muscle." You've heard it at the gym.

ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) say otherwise. Guideline 8: get good-quality protein from a combination of foods, and avoid protein supplements to build muscle mass.

Dal with rice or roti, milk and curd, eggs, paneer, fish and chicken can cover a healthy adult's needs (0.83 g per kg of body weight a day).

If you have a medical condition, follow your doctor's advice.
posts.cta_line: Our free guide shows how to reach your number with food. Link in bio.
posts.alt: Photo of a bowl of dal and rice. Glass card: 'Protein powder to build muscle? ICMR-NIN advises against it. Combine foods instead.'

posts.hook: Three Indian breakfasts, protein counted
posts.ig:
Three everyday Indian breakfasts, with the protein counted from ICMR-NIN's Indian Food Composition Tables.

2 rotis (60 g atta) and a bowl of dal (30 g raw): about 13 g.
1 egg and a glass of milk (200 ml): about 14 g.
50 g paneer bhurji with 2 rotis: about 15 g.

For a 60 kg adult, the daily need is about 50 g (0.83 g per kg), so breakfast can carry a good share.

posts.hook: About eight glasses a day
posts.ig:
Winter makes it easy to forget water.

ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) say a normal healthy person needs about eight glasses, roughly two litres, of water a day, including other drinks.

Keep a bottle where you can see it, and have a glass with every meal.
posts.cta_line: More everyday numbers in our free guide. Link in bio.
posts.li:
A small reminder for winter: ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) put a healthy adult's need at about eight glasses (around two litres) of water a day, including other beverages.

In offices with heating and long meetings, it's often the first habit to slip.

posts.hook: 30 minutes, five days a week
posts.ig:
How much should you move? ICMR-NIN gives a number.

The Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) recommend that adults do 30 to 60 minutes of moderate activity a day, on at least five days a week. For children and teenagers, it's at least 60 minutes a day.

A brisk walk counts. So do climbing the stairs, cycling, dancing at a wedding and playing with the kids.

ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024): 30 to 60 minutes of moderate activity a day, on at least five days a week, for adults. At least 60 minutes a day for children aged 5 to 19.

It's one of the few health targets that needs no equipment. A brisk walk counts.

posts.hook: National Milk Day: 300 ml of milk or curd
posts.ig:
It's National Milk Day, marked on Dr Verghese Kurien's birth anniversary.

ICMR-NIN's My Plate for the Day includes 300 ml of milk or curd, which gives about 10 g of protein. That's a glass of milk and a katori of dahi.

If you're vegetarian, milk and curd are among the easiest ways to improve the quality of your protein.

posts.hook: Read any Indian food label in four steps
posts.ig:
Most packaged food in India carries four things FSSAI requires. Here's what to look at, in order.

1. The veg or non-veg symbol.
2. The FSSAI logo and licence number.
3. The ingredient list, in order of weight.
4. The nutrition information, per 100 g or per pack.

If you'd like to understand food standards in depth, NNWA's Food Science & FSSAI course is 100% online.
posts.li:
FSSAI's Labelling and Display Regulations (2020) require four things on most packaged foods: the veg or non-veg symbol, the FSSAI logo and licence number, an ingredient list in descending order of weight, and nutrition information.

Teaching clients to read those four is one of the most useful half-hours in nutrition counselling. NNWA's Food Science & FSSAI course goes much further.

posts.hook: Swap, don't stop
posts.ig:
Four swaps straight from ICMR-NIN's Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024).

Deep-fried snacks: try nuts and seeds.
Fruit juice: eat the whole fruit.
Refined, high-sugar sweets: choose traditional sweets made with whole grains, millets, nuts and oilseeds.
Sugary drinks: buttermilk, lemon water or tender coconut water.

No food is banned. Small swaps add up.
